source.title: Polysemantic Experts, Monosemantic Paths: Routing as Control in MoEs
source.authors: Charles Ye; Bo Yuan; Lee Sharkey

record.tranche_reason: The study argues for a refinement of the unit of interpretation in MoEs: it reports that expert paths cluster by semantic function even though individual experts are described as polysemantic. Its results concern paths and hidden-state clusters, not neuron-level polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The paper asserts that individual experts remain polysemantic, but does not directly measure whether an individual neuron or expert responds to unrelated inputs. Its own relevant results are path-level semantic clustering and comparisons of hidden-state cluster diversity. Cited prior findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study analyses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing: expert paths and hidden-state subspace clusters. It asserts, citing prior work, that individual experts are polysemantic, but never measures how often or how strongly experts or MLP neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Experts are not neurons, and paths are a different unit, so no version (V1–V7) is tested. The record's 'tests/T5' contradicts its own finding that every version is not_tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that expert paths, not individual experts, are monosemantic, and that the trajectory is the natural unit of interpretability in MoEs. The record should note that the claim 'individual experts remain polysemantic' rests on cited prior work and is not measured in this study.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an SVD-based router-visible/router-blind decomposition, probes, and clustering of expert paths; it does not use the original vision-neuron analysis method.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-layer top-1 expert paths in MoE language models group tokens by semantic function across languages and surface forms. Clusters in the router-visible subspace contain about 4x more unique token IDs (4.3) than router-blind (1.1) or full hidden-state (1.4) clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE language models, units that are polysemantic at a single layer (experts) compose across layers into paths that are semantically coherent, so the unit of analysis determines apparent monosemanticity.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align)
record.problems: The reported path-level semantic examples are qualitative. The cluster comparison uses 100 sampled clusters and 10 token samples per cluster, filters approximately 5% rated uninterpretable by automated scoring, and does not directly measure individual-neuron or individual-expert response polysemanticity. Uncertainty for the cluster-diversity values is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results omitted. Router prediction probes, surface-feature probes, and routing-weight correlations concern routing mechanics rather than neuron polysemanticity or path semantic coherence.

untested.parts: Share of MLP neurons in language models responding to unrelated tokens. Expert polysemanticity is only asserted from cited work (Jiang 2024, Xue 2024, etc.), not measured.
Superposition as the cause; not studied.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure; not studied.
Dependence on architecture or training. The study spans six MoE architectures but measures no polysemanticity share in any of them.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature. Path-level monosemanticity concerns a different unit and does not resolve individual neurons or experts.
Measurement dependence of neuron polysemanticity; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from tests/T5 to discusses/T6: no row measures neuron or expert polysemanticity. The probe, correlation and rotation results (Sections 3, D–F) concern routing mechanics and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: MLP neurons in transformer language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts; the study analyzes MoE expert paths and hidden-state clusters instead.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons due to activation, architecture, or regularization, and associated performance costs.

Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related jobs; the study reports semantic organization of multi-layer expert paths, not a resolution of individual neurons or experts' mixed responses.
Whether neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation-scoring method.

rows.subject: QWEN3-30B-A3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared top-1 expert paths for the token “:” across three syntactic roles.

conditions.value: Python type annotation; introductory colon; time separator
Balanced role representation using auxiliary LLM-generated text

rows.measure: Visual and textual comparison of multi-layer expert trajectories across roles.
rows.value: The three uses produce visibly distinct expert trajectories.
rows.note: The text reports distinct paths for the same token in different contextual functions; it does not measure individual-neuron responses.
rows.check: Qualitative path visualisation for the ':' token in Qwen3. No baseline or number is given. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: GPT-OSS-20B
rows.operation_detail: Grouped tokens sharing identical top-1 expert paths across a contiguous mid-layer band.

conditions.value: Approximately 10M multilingual tokens from C4 and HPLT; EN/ZH/ES

rows.measure: Semantic coherence of token groups sharing an expert path.
rows.value: Groups are described as tightly coherent across languages and surface forms; examples include exhibition-related, overseas, nutritional-substance, and brand-name groups.
rows.note: The authors describe these examples as representative of thousands of similarly coherent groups. This is path-level evidence, not a measurement of neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Qualitative examples of coherent path groups. 'Thousands of similarly coherent groups' is asserted, not quantified. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: GPT-OSS-20B
rows.operation_detail: Clustered tokens in the router-visible control subspace across layers, then measured unique token IDs per cluster.

conditions.value: 100 sampled cross-layer clusters; k=32 per layer
10 token samples per cluster; approximately 5% rated uninterpretable were filtered

rows.measure: Mean unique token IDs per cluster among retained interpretable clusters.
rows.baseline: Content clusters: 1.1 unique token IDs per cluster; full hidden-state clusters: 1.4.
rows.note: The paper describes the control-subspace clusters as grouping more diverse tokens by shared function, and states that all three subspaces had at least 95% pass screening.
rows.check: Valid study result (4.3 unique IDs per h_vis cluster), but it concerns subspace clusters, not neurons.

rows.subject: GPT-OSS-20B
rows.operation_detail: Clustered tokens in the router-blind content channel across layers, then measured unique token IDs per cluster.

conditions.value: 100 sampled cross-layer clusters; k=32 per layer
10 token samples per cluster; approximately 5% rated uninterpretable were filtered

rows.measure: Mean unique token IDs per cluster among retained interpretable clusters.
rows.baseline: Router-visible control clusters: 4.3 unique token IDs per cluster.
rows.note: The authors characterize these clusters as coherent but largely composed of repeated instances of the same token.
rows.check: Comparator row whose 'partial' state has no version to refer to. 1.1 unique token IDs per h_blind cluster is a cluster lexical-diversity measure, not a polysemanticity rate.

rows.subject: GPT-OSS-20B
rows.operation_detail: Clustered tokens in the full hidden state across layers, then measured unique token IDs per cluster.

conditions.value: 100 sampled cross-layer clusters; k=32 per layer
10 token samples per cluster; approximately 5% rated uninterpretable were filtered

rows.measure: Mean unique token IDs per cluster among retained interpretable clusters.
rows.baseline: Router-visible control clusters: 4.3 unique token IDs per cluster.
rows.note: The authors report a pattern similar to the content clusters, with low lexical diversity.
rows.check: Comparator row whose 'partial' state has no version to refer to. 1.4 unique IDs per full-hidden-state cluster says nothing about neuron polysemanticity.
